title: The Thief Who Robbed His Own Shadow (ES)
summary: A burglar flees in terror from his own shadow on a moonlit night. Birbal uses the incident to explain how guilt terrifies itself. [ES]
full_text:
In the middle of a clear, moonlit night, an imperial night watchman in Agra noticed a man sprinting frantically through the alleys, screaming in terror, repeatedly drawing his dagger and stabbing at the ground behind him!

The guards tackled the frantic man and brought him to the palace guardhouse.

The prisoner was an infamous burglar named Kallu, and in his pouch were three stolen diamond necklaces looted from a merchant's mansion an hour earlier.

When Emperor Akbar questioned the thief next morning: 'Why were you running and screaming like a madman if you had successfully escaped the merchant's guards?'

Kallu shivered: 'Sire, a dark, terrifying demon was chasing me through the streets! Wherever I ran, he ran behind me! When I jumped, he leaped! When I drew my dagger, he raised a blade to strike me! I was fighting for my life against a phantom of the underworld!'

Birbal smiled, walked to the open archway where the morning sun cast long shadows across the floor, and said:

'Kallu, look behind you right now! The demon is standing beside you!'

Kallu screamed and leaped away—only to see his own dark shadow moving across the marble floor!

The entire court burst into laughter.

Birbal explained to Emperor Akbar:

'Sire, the moonlight was bright last night. When Kallu committed the burglary, his guilty conscience terrified his mind.

'When he saw his own long, dark shadow stretching behind him under the street lamps, his guilt transformed his harmless shadow into an avenging officer of justice! He was running from his own reflection, fighting his own hands!

'A righteous man sleeps in peace under the stars, feared by none and fearing nothing. But the thief carries his own executioner inside his breast; even his own shadow becomes an army that drives him into chains.'

Akbar commended Birbal's psychological wisdom, sentencing the burglar while reflecting upon the inescapable terror of guilt.
